title: Fixed time-asymmetric correlations with arbitrarily weak dissipation
oneLine: One fixed time-asymmetric covariance is shared by Markov models with every positive entropy-production rate, so its Gaussian value, 1/3, is not the lower bound on dissipation that Seara, Machta and Murrell (2021) stated for nonlinear systems.
abstract: Experiments often estimate how much energy a living or driven system dissipates from the time asymmetry of its measured correlations. A popular shortcut assigns the observed covariance the entropy-production rate of a Gaussian process with the same covariance, and Seara, Machta and Murrell (Nature Communications 12, 392, 2021) stated that this gives a lower bound for nonlinear systems as well. This candidate shows that it does not. A family of fully observed four-state Markov chains shares one fixed, nonzero, time-asymmetric covariance at every lag, with bounded transition rates and uniform mixing, while their entropy-production rates take every positive value. Fully observed planar Markov diffusions with linear drift and state-dependent noise have exactly the same covariance, with entropy-production rates filling (0, 1/3], where 1/3 is the Gaussian value; a Student-type member has rate α/(3(α+1)). In both cases rare, large excursions carry the covariance. A reversible-gating construction gives the general mechanism, the paper locates the missing step in the published justification, and an established fourth-order bound recovers up to 93.5% of the exact rate on the example. Weak dissipation at fixed covariance needs growing amplitudes or heavy-tailed noise, and diffusions with constant noise remain open. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Four-state chains with one fixed covariance C(t) = e^{Ft}Σ at every lag, bounded rates, uniform mixing and an injective readout have entropy-production rates ε log((6−κ)/(3−κ)) covering (0, ∞) (Theorem 1, proof with exact checks).

The Gaussian spectral value of that covariance is exactly 1/3, so it is not a lower bound; at (ε, κ) = (1/4, 1) the true rate is log(5/2)/4 ≈ 0.229 and the overestimate is unbounded in general; the failure persists for bounded readouts, sampled and smoothed records (Section 3 and Section 8, proof).

Planar diffusions with the Gaussian comparator’s linear drift and state-dependent noise reproduce the same covariance with entropy-production rates filling (0, 1/3]; a Student-type member has rate α/(3(α+1)) (Theorem 2, Proposition 3, proof).
Reversible gating preserves any centred covariance while multiplying entropy production by ε (Theorem 4, Corollary 5, proof).
The Raux–Maier–Seifert fourth-order bound recovers 6/(7 log(5/2)) ≈ 93.5% of the exact rate at short lags; a naive kurtosis-discounted bound fails in a random search (Section 6, proof and numerics).
Open: whether a diffusion with constant noise and nonlinear drift can reproduce the covariance with dissipation below 1/3.

narration: Same correlations, any dissipation. An Evidence Press briefing. First, the problem. Living and driven systems, like molecular motors or chemical clocks, constantly use energy, and scientists want to know how much. Measuring it directly is hard, so they often look at a few recorded signals instead. If one signal tends to follow another more than the reverse, the system is running irreversibly, and so it must be using energy. A popular shortcut converts these correlations into a number by pretending the signals come from the simplest random process with the same correlations, a Gaussian process. A 2021 paper in Nature Communications stated that, for nonlinear systems, this Gaussian number is a lower bound on the true energy use. The main finding is that this lower-bound statement is false. The paper builds simple models that have exactly the same correlations at every time delay, yet use energy at any rate at all. For a family of four-state models the rate can be any positive value, and for a family of smooth two-dimensional random motions it can be anything between zero and the Gaussian value of one third. The reason is intuitive. Imagine a system that is idle almost all the time and only occasionally bursts into fast circulation. Rare, large bursts can carry the whole correlation signal, while energy is only spent during the bursts. Why it matters: a correlation measurement alone cannot certify a minimum energy cost. Extra information helps; a published fourth-order bound recovers up to ninety-three point five per cent of the true value in the example. The limits: the examples need growing signal sizes or very uneven noise, short recordings may miss the bursts, and smooth motions with constant noise remain an open case. This is an anonymous, unrefereed candidate, checked by AI-assisted review only, not peer review. Published on 28 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Fully observed four-state Markov chains and planar diffusions sharing one fixed time-asymmetric covariance with arbitrarily small entropy production refute the unrestricted Gaussian lower-bound statement of Seara, Machta and Murrell (2021).
